strengths: Establishes rigorous theoretical framework for lossless vocabulary reduction with well-derived theorems and proofs
Natural and meaningful generalization of prior byte-level reduction work to arbitrary sub-vocabularies
Provides both exact and efficient approximate algorithms with practical top-K optimization
Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 model families and 4 datasets with detailed ablations
Clear presentation with well-motivated problem and illustrative examples (Figure 2)
Demonstrates practical application to model ensemble with consistent performance across multiple configurations
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty—the extension from bytes to sub-vocabularies is a straightforward generalization; nested tokenization, while elegant, is an intuitive composition of existing concepts

Significant gap between theory and practice: even with equivalent text distributions, greedy decoding produces different outputs (Section B demonstrates 000 vs 001 generation despite identical distributions)
Algorithm 2's top-K approximation lacks theoretical guarantees, convergence bounds, or principled guidance for setting K (requires K≥250-1250 depending on task, Section D.7)
Modest empirical improvements: ensemble results often marginal (MMLU-Pro 42.00 vs best single 42.71), and some cases underperform baselines (Table 1 Falcon3-7B anomalies)
Computational overhead not thoroughly analyzed: D.7.3 shows non-negligible counts during generation; wall-clock comparisons against full-vocabulary models absent
Validity assumption (Eq. 7) is not empirically verified; no analysis of robustness if condition violated
Limited scope: primary application is 2-model ensemble; scalability and other mentioned applications (speculative decoding, distillation) unexplored
Weak experimental baselines: naive restriction is trivial; no comparison with other vocabulary reduction methods from related work

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework with formal theorems proving losslessness at the distribution level (Theorem 3.1)
Practical algorithmic contributions including both exact (Algorithm 1) and approximate (Algorithm 2) methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (Qwen, OLMo, Llama, Falcon, etc.) and benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, ACP, MMLU-Pro, translation)
Clear illustrative examples and worked cases that help explain abstract concepts
Extensive ablation studies on hyperparameter K and additional experiments in appendix
weaknesses: Critical issue: 'Lossless' claim is misleading—Section B and D.4 explicitly show greedy decoding produces different outputs despite identical text distributions, contradicting practical losslessness. The theoretical guarantee only holds in expectation over random samples, not for deterministic greedy decoding used in practice.

Limited novelty—primarily a generalization of Phan et al. (2025) from bytes to arbitrary sub-vocabularies using similar theoretical techniques (validity conditions, minimal covers, recursive formulas)

Weak empirical improvements: vocabulary reduction results mixed (some show worse performance like Llama 25.93 vs 26.00), ensemble improvements marginal or worse than byte-level baseline (Table 2: MCV 81.12 vs 1-byte 82.49)
Top-K approximation in Algorithm 2 is significantly lossy—Table 13 shows random sampling completely fails (K=1: 78.09 vs original 47.54), undermining 'losslessness' claim
Unclear practical motivation: no advantage demonstrated over simpler byte-level ensemble, and maximal common vocabulary can be very small (63,552 of 151,665 tokens in one case)
Limited scope of applications: only model ensemble demonstrated despite introduction mentioning knowledge distillation, speculative decoding, and inference-time alignment
Presentation concerns: dense notation, greedy decoding inconsistency buried in footnotes, central claims insufficiently qualified
Experimental design: naive restriction baseline is strawman (sets out-of-vocab to 0), no comparison with embedding-similarity or string-matching heuristics mentioned in related work
Missing analyses: computational cost largely relegated to appendix, no memory analysis, no failure case analysis, scalability to very large vocabularies unexplored
Hyperparameter choices not well justified (e.g., K=300 when Table 12 shows K=1 often sufficient for greedy decoding)

strengths: Novel theoretical framework that elegantly generalizes byte-level vocabulary reduction to arbitrary sub-vocabularies through nested tokenization
Rigorous mathematical formulation with sound proofs of lossless property (Theorem 3.1) and recursive computation (Theorem 3.4)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (6 architectures), benchmarks (4 datasets), and ablation studies
Both theoretical (exact Algorithm 1) and practical (efficient Algorithm 2) implementations with demonstrated speedup (1.8-2.0× faster than byte-level ensemble)
Clear exposition with effective illustrative examples and thorough appendices enabling reproducibility
Principled approach to ensemble learning via maximal common vocabulary with theoretical guarantees
weaknesses: Approximation algorithm (Algorithm 2) lacks theoretical error bounds; top-K filtering is heuristic with no principled justification for K=300 choice
Practical improvements are modest and inconsistent—vocabulary reduction results often within 1% of naive baselines, ensemble gains mixed across benchmarks
Greedy decoding produces different text from equivalent distributions despite theoretical losslessness; paper acknowledges but provides no mitigation strategy, undermining practical deployment
Limited novelty over Phan et al. (2025)—core concepts (validity condition, relative covers) are generalizations of existing work rather than fundamentally new insights
Application scope limited to model ensemble; promised applications (speculative decoding, distillation, inference-time alignment) unexplored
Maximal common vocabulary can be very small (Table 10: 32,932/63,992 tokens for some pairs); systematic analysis of MCV size impact on performance missing
Baseline quality concerns—Union baseline achieves implausibly low 1.93% on MMLU-Pro; no significance testing or error bars provided across experimental runs
Computational overhead analysis incomplete—Table 3 shows relative speedup vs byte-level but no absolute latency comparison to unreduced models
